title: Landing Page or Full Website? How to Decide What Your Business Actually Needs
excerpt: Many businesses over-invest in a full site they don't need — or under-invest with a landing page that limits their growth. Here's how to make the right call.

blocks.text: You're starting a new project, launching a service, or finally getting your business online. Someone tells you to 'just build a landing page'. Someone else says you need a proper website. You're not sure who to listen to.

This is one of the most common — and most expensive — decisions early-stage businesses get wrong. Over-invest in a full website before you need it and you've burned budget and months of time. Under-invest with a landing page that can't scale and you'll be rebuilding in 12 months anyway.
The right answer depends on where you are, what you're selling, and what you need the site to do. Here's a clear framework for making that call.
What Is a Landing Page?
A landing page is a single, focused web page with one goal: get the visitor to take one specific action. Sign up. Buy. Book a call. Register interest.

It has no navigation menu. No blog. No 'About' section. Everything on the page exists to push the visitor toward that single conversion. That's what makes it powerful for specific campaigns — and limited as a long-term business asset.
What Is a Full Website?

A full website is a multi-page structure covering your services, about page, contact page, and often a blog or resource section. It serves multiple audiences at different stages of the buying journey — from someone who's never heard of you to someone ready to purchase.
A full website can rank in search engines for multiple terms, build authority over time, and grow with your business. It requires more upfront investment but creates a compounding asset.
When a Landing Page Is the Right Choice
A landing page is the right tool when you have a single, defined conversion goal and a direct traffic source driving visitors to it. Specifically:

items: **Product or service launch:** You're validating demand before committing to a full build
**Paid ad campaigns:** You're running Google or Meta ads and need a focused destination that matches your ad copy
**Pre-launch email collection:** You want to build a waitlist before you go live
**A/B testing:** You're testing messaging, pricing, or offers before scaling
**Event or webinar sign-ups:** A single date, a single action
**One specific product:** You sell one thing and want all attention on that one conversion

blocks.text: The pattern here: you control where the traffic comes from, and that traffic has a clear intent. A landing page converts that intent efficiently.
**Takeaway:** If you're spending money on ads or have a clear, single campaign goal, a landing page is usually faster and more cost-effective than a full site.
When You Need a Full Website
A full website becomes necessary when your business is more complex, your buyer journey is longer, or you're relying on organic discovery rather than paid traffic. The clearest signals:

items: **Multiple services or offerings:** Visitors need to navigate to what's relevant to them
**Long consideration cycles:** Your buyers research for days or weeks before contacting you (B2B, high-ticket services)
**SEO is part of your strategy:** You need multiple pages to rank for different keywords
**Authority and credibility matter:** Clients need case studies, testimonials, and a clear picture of who you are before they trust you
**Content publishing:** You're building a blog, resource centre, or knowledge base
**Multiple audiences:** You serve different types of clients with different needs

blocks.text: If someone searches for your service in Google and lands on your site, a one-page landing page often isn't enough. They want to understand who you are, see your past work, read about your process, and find answers to their questions — across multiple pages.
**Takeaway:** If you depend on organic search, serve multiple audiences, or sell something that requires trust before purchase, you need a full website.
The Cost and Time Difference
The investment gap between a landing page and a full website is significant. Here's a realistic comparison:

These aren't arbitrary figures. A professional landing page — properly designed, copywritten, and optimised — costs €800–2,500 and can be live within one to two weeks. A full website with five or more pages, SEO-ready structure, and content takes considerably longer and costs more.

The mistake is treating the lower cost of a landing page as a saving when what you actually need is a full site. You'll spend €1,500 now and €8,000 in six months, rather than €8,000 now. That's not saving money — that's spending more.
The SEO Trap to Avoid
Here's the single most common strategic mistake we see: a business builds a landing page, starts to grow, then realises they need SEO — and discovers the landing page is nearly useless for it.

Search engines rank pages, not just domains. To build topical authority — the kind that earns first-page rankings — you need multiple pages, each targeting different keywords, supported by a content strategy that signals expertise to Google.

A single landing page can rank for exactly one phrase, and usually not very competitively. You can't build a blog section on a landing page. You can't add case studies, service subpages, or an FAQ section that attracts long-tail search traffic.

If SEO is anywhere in your 12-month plan, build a proper site from the start. The domain authority you build in months one through six compounds into your rankings in months 12 through 24. Starting over later means losing that entire compounding period.
**Takeaway:** A landing page cannot build topical authority. If organic search is part of your growth plan, you need a real site foundation now — not later.
The Practical Middle Path
Most early-stage businesses don't need a 20-page website. But they do need more than a landing page. The practical answer is a lean four-page site: Home, Services, About, and Contact.

This gives you enough structure to rank in search, build credibility with visitors, and present your full offer — without the cost and time of a large build. A lean four-page site typically costs €3,000–5,000 and takes three to five weeks to launch.

The critical advantage of building this on a proper architecture — like Next.js rather than a website builder — is that it's genuinely expandable. Add a services subpage in month two. Add a blog in month six. Add case studies in month nine. You're not rebuilding; you're extending.
A landing page built on Webflow or Squarespace, by contrast, requires a platform migration when you outgrow it. You lose accumulated SEO authority and start again.
**Takeaway:** A lean four-page site on a proper technical foundation costs more than a landing page upfront but far less than two builds. It grows with you.
A Quick Decision Framework
Use this table to map your situation to the right solution:

Early stage, limited budget, no SEO plans

blocks.text: The majority of businesses asking this question are established enough that they need a full site. They're just underestimating how quickly they'll hit the limits of a landing page.
